title: The SAP-C03 architecture journey
lead: Work from requirements to an architecture that can survive scrutiny across five exam domains.
points: Cloud architecture and AI integration: 25%
Security, compliance and governance: 25%
Cost optimization: 15%
Resilience, migration and continuity: 15%
Operational excellence and automation: 20%
takeaway: A strong answer meets every stated constraint, including ownership, failure tolerance, cost and operational effort.

title: How to read an architecture question
lead: Separate facts from implied preferences before comparing services.
points: Underline hard constraints such as RTO, RPO, residency, latency and existing licenses.
Identify the traffic path, trust boundary, data lifecycle and who operates each component.
Eliminate choices that violate a hard constraint before optimizing cost or convenience.
When several options work, prefer the design with the fewest unnecessary moving parts.
takeaway: The exam tests architectural judgment, not isolated product recall.

title: One scenario, five architecture lenses
lead: An international customer portal needs secure sign-in, regional data controls and a 30-minute recovery target.
points: Design: choose services around access patterns and latency.
Security: trace each identity and data boundary.
Cost: include replication, requests and inter-Region transfer.
Resilience: prove recovery with dependencies and a tested runbook.
Operations: make changes repeatable and observable.
takeaway: A solution that satisfies four lenses but ignores a fifth remains incomplete.

title: The study loop for every module
lead: Learn the mechanism, compare neighboring choices, then test a realistic constraint change.
points: Trace the request and control plane in the diagram.
Explain why the nearest alternative fails in a concrete scenario.
Use a decision exercise to apply the idea under pressure.
Revisit mistakes after adjacent modules add new services or constraints.
takeaway: The following identity module starts with authorization because every later architecture depends on it.

title: Identity decisions begin with the principal
lead: A request succeeds only when the right principal can perform the right action on the right resource in the relevant context.
points: Name the human, application, AWS service or external machine that makes the call.
Identify which credentials that principal actually presents.
Locate the identity policy, resource policy and any guardrails that apply.
Check the requested action, resource ARN and condition values together.
takeaway: A service diagram without identities cannot explain its security model.

title: IAM identities and credential lifetimes
lead: Choose credentials according to where the caller runs and how long it needs access.
points: IAM roles provide temporary credentials to trusted principals and workloads.
IAM users may have long-term credentials and need stricter lifecycle controls.
An assumed-role session has its own session identity and expiration.
The account root user is for account-level tasks and should not run workloads.
takeaway: Design a short-lived session path before considering a permanent access key.

title: The anatomy of a policy statement
lead: Effect, Action, Resource and Condition jointly define a grant or denial.
points: Effect is Allow or Deny; an explicit Deny wins over applicable Allows.
Action matches API operations, while Resource scopes supported ARNs.
Condition checks request context such as tags, principal attributes or network origin.
Principal appears in resource-based and trust policies to identify who is covered.
takeaway: Read the entire statement; a broad action can still be narrowed by a meaningful condition.

title: Allow, implicit deny and explicit deny
lead: Start with default denial. A matching Allow can grant access only if no applicable explicit Deny blocks it.
points: No matching Allow produces an implicit deny.
A matching explicit Deny takes precedence across evaluated policies.
A guardrail can also withhold permission through its allowed maximum.
Do not treat a missing Allow as interchangeable with an explicit Deny in cross-account analysis.
takeaway: Identify the exact statement or boundary responsible for the result.

title: Identity policies and resource policies
lead: Identity policies attach to principals. Resource policies attach to supported resources and name a principal.
points: An identity policy expresses what its principal can request.
A resource policy can grant another principal access to a specific resource.
Within one account, an applicable Allow can come from either side, subject to evaluation rules.
Cross-account access commonly requires permission on the caller side and permission on the target side.
takeaway: For cross-account questions, analyze both accounts and the kind of principal named by the resource policy.

title: Permissions boundaries limit delegated IAM
lead: A boundary sets the maximum permissions an IAM user or role can receive through identity policies.
points: The identity policy must allow an action, and the boundary must permit it.
A boundary does not grant access by itself.
Use a boundary when teams may create roles but must stay within a central ceiling.
Resource policy grants to particular principal types have nuanced evaluation; check the named ARN.
takeaway: A role creator cannot exceed a boundary merely by attaching an AdministratorAccess policy.

title: SCPs, RCPs and delegated permissions
lead: Organization policies define account-level ceilings; they are separate from grants inside the account.
points: An SCP restricts the maximum permissions for principals in a member account.
An RCP restricts maximum permissions for resources in member accounts where supported.
Neither policy grants an action by itself.
Account-level design still requires IAM and resource policies to supply the actual Allow.
takeaway: A permissive IAM policy cannot overcome a restrictive organization guardrail.

title: Session policies narrow a role session
lead: A session policy passed to STS can reduce permissions for one assumed-role session.
points: The role identity policy remains the maximum starting point for the session.
The session policy intersects with that role permission set.
Use it to scope an otherwise shared role to a request, tenant or job.
A session policy never expands the role's effective permissions.
takeaway: The same role can issue differently constrained sessions without creating a new permanent role each time.

title: Cross-account role assumption
lead: Account A's caller assumes a role in Account B, then uses the resulting session to access B's resources.
points: A policy on A's caller permits sts:AssumeRole for the target role.
B's role trust policy accepts the caller principal and any required conditions.
STS issues credentials for B's role session after trust and authorization checks.
The role's permission policies and B's guardrails govern subsequent resource calls.
takeaway: The trust policy controls who can become the role; the permissions policy controls what that role can do.

title: Trust policies and the confused deputy
lead: A third-party service operates for many customers and needs a role in your account.
points: Trust only the provider principal that must assume the role.
Require a unique external ID agreed with that provider for the customer context.
Grant the role only the actions and resources the integration needs.
Confirm the provider supplies the correct external ID on every AssumeRole request.
takeaway: An external ID helps prevent a provider from using one customer's role on another customer's behalf; it is not a password replacement.

title: Role chaining and session boundaries
lead: When one assumed role assumes another, trace the session identity at every hop.
points: Each hop has a new trust-policy check.
Permission to call sts:AssumeRole must exist at the current hop.
Session duration and session policy restrictions can matter when roles are chained.
Avoid unnecessary chains that complicate attribution and expiration.
takeaway: Follow the credentials actually used for the final request, not the human's original permissions.

title: ABAC with principal and resource tags
lead: Attribute-based access control uses context instead of enumerating every resource ARN.
points: A policy can compare a principal tag such as Project with a matching resource tag.
Control who may set and change those tags; otherwise tags become a privilege-escalation path.
Use session tags when a federated identity supplies verified attributes.
Check whether the service and action support the condition keys you intend to use.
takeaway: ABAC scales access patterns only when tag provenance is trustworthy.

title: Service roles and service-linked roles
lead: AWS services may need a role to act in your account, but the role's purpose and lifecycle differ.
points: A service role is configured for a workload or service integration and has a trust relationship.
A service-linked role is associated with a specific AWS service and uses predefined service expectations.
Inspect what the service assumes and what resources it may change.
Do not replace a workload identity with an overly broad shared role.
takeaway: Trace service-to-service access as a principal chain, just like human access.

title: IAM Identity Center for workforce access
lead: Centralize workforce access to multiple AWS accounts and applications.
points: An external identity provider or the Identity Center directory supplies workforce users and groups.
Permission sets define access that Identity Center provisions into target accounts.
Assignments connect a user or group with a permission set and an account.
Users sign in through the portal or supported command-line flow to receive temporary access.
takeaway: An account assignment and a permission set solve different parts of the authorization path.

title: SAML federation for workforce sign-in
lead: A SAML identity provider asserts that a user authenticated and supplies attributes for the AWS access path.
points: The identity provider authenticates the person and issues a signed SAML assertion.
AWS validates the trusted provider relationship and maps the assertion to an authorized role or application.
Role sessions provide temporary AWS credentials when AWS API access is required.
Separate sign-in, provisioning and authorization; SAML authentication alone does not grant every account.
takeaway: When the problem says workforce SSO across accounts, begin with Identity Center and the enterprise IdP.

title: SCIM provisioning is a lifecycle channel
lead: SCIM synchronizes identities and groups; SAML handles authentication assertions.
points: Provision users and groups from the external directory into Identity Center with SCIM.
Disable or update identities centrally when employees move or leave.
Use SAML or another configured sign-in method to authenticate sessions.
Keep group assignments aligned with least-privilege permission sets.
takeaway: A provisioned user still needs a sign-in path and an access assignment.

title: OIDC identity tokens and trust
lead: An OIDC provider supplies signed tokens that AWS can validate for a configured federation flow.
points: Verify issuer, audience and subject claims against the role's trust conditions.
Use narrow subject claims to bind a workload or application to the intended role.
Exchange a valid token for temporary AWS credentials only when the workload needs AWS API access.
A token for the wrong audience should not be trusted for this role.
takeaway: Issuer identity alone is insufficient; audience and subject commonly decide whether a token belongs to this workload.

title: Choose the federation entry point
lead: Workforce users, application customers and external machines have different identity lifecycles.
points: Workforce access across accounts: IAM Identity Center with the enterprise directory.
Customer sign-in to an application: Cognito user pool or a compatible external application IdP.
AWS API calls on behalf of authenticated customers: Cognito identity pool where appropriate.
Servers outside AWS: IAM Roles Anywhere or supported OIDC federation based on the trust model.
takeaway: The right federation product depends first on who the principal is.

title: Cognito user pools authenticate app users
lead: A user pool provides an application user directory and issues tokens after sign-in.
points: Users authenticate through a native flow or a configured external provider.
The application validates tokens and uses claims to decide what its own APIs permit.
OAuth 2.0 authorization flows support delegated access patterns.
User-pool tokens are not themselves long-term IAM access keys.
takeaway: Choose a user pool for application sign-in and token-based authorization at the app layer.

title: Cognito identity pools broker AWS access
lead: An identity pool maps authenticated or supported guest identities to temporary IAM role credentials.
points: The application first obtains a supported identity token when authentication is required.
The identity pool selects an authorized IAM role and obtains temporary credentials.
The client can then call allowed AWS APIs directly under that role's policies.
Limit the role to the needed resources and account for untrusted client environments.
takeaway: User pools answer who signed in; identity pools answer how an eligible client gets limited AWS credentials.

title: OAuth 2.0 roles in an application design
lead: OAuth separates the client requesting delegated access from the resource server that enforces it.
points: An authorization server issues tokens for the intended audience and scopes.
The API checks token validity, audience, expiry and the requested scope.
An application role or fine-grained policy can further restrict tenant data access.
Do not mistake an OAuth scope for an IAM permission unless a deliberate bridge maps one to the other.
takeaway: Application authorization and AWS IAM authorization operate at different boundaries.

title: The application authorization boundary
lead: A customer token says tenant A, but the request asks for tenant B's report.
points: Authenticate the token and confirm its intended API audience.
Derive tenant identity from trusted claims or server-side mapping, not a client-supplied path alone.
Authorize the report against that tenant before reading the underlying S3 object or database row.
Use IAM to limit the API service's infrastructure access separately.
takeaway: A valid sign-in does not imply permission to every application's data record.

title: EKS Pod Identity for AWS API calls
lead: Associate a Kubernetes service account with an IAM role so a pod obtains scoped AWS credentials.
points: The pod uses the configured Pod Identity integration to obtain temporary credentials.
The role trust relationship allows the EKS Pod Identity service to assume it.
The role policy grants only the AWS APIs that workload needs.
Restrict access to node credentials; otherwise a pod may reach a broader node role.
takeaway: Give each workload the role it needs instead of sharing a powerful node identity.

title: Workload identity on EC2, ECS and Lambda
lead: Managed compute environments can supply temporary credentials through an attached role.
points: EC2 instance profiles expose an associated role to applications on the instance.
ECS task roles scope access to a task instead of the whole container instance.
A Lambda execution role governs the function's calls to AWS services.
Keep the trust policy aligned with the service and the permission policy aligned with the application.
takeaway: Choose the narrowest workload identity boundary that the compute platform supports.

title: IAM Roles Anywhere for outside workloads
lead: A server outside AWS can exchange X.509 credentials for temporary AWS role credentials.
points: A trust anchor establishes the certificate authority that AWS will trust.
A profile controls which IAM roles and session settings the workload can use.
The workload proves certificate possession and receives temporary credentials.
Plan certificate issuance, rotation and revocation as part of the architecture.
takeaway: Roles Anywhere replaces static AWS keys for suitable external workloads but requires disciplined PKI operations.

title: Hybrid and multi-cloud identity trade-offs
lead: Choose a bridge that your existing workload platform can authenticate reliably.
points: AWS-hosted workloads generally use their platform's managed IAM role integration.
External workloads with managed X.509 identity can use Roles Anywhere.
An external OIDC issuer can federate when claims and trust policies identify the workload precisely.
Avoid distributing static access keys to every server during a migration.
takeaway: The trust root and credential rotation path matter more than a short initial setup.

title: Resource access across account boundaries
lead: A central analytics account needs to read one bucket in a workload account.
points: Option A: assume a narrowly scoped role in the workload account and read as that session.
Option B: grant a specific external principal in the bucket policy, with caller-side authorization.
Account for KMS key permissions if the objects use a customer managed key.
Use organization IDs or other precise conditions where supported to avoid broad sharing.
takeaway: Object access and KMS decryption are separate authorization decisions.

title: Data perimeters and trusted context
lead: A data perimeter limits which identities, resources and network origins can interact with protected data.
points: Define trusted principals, resources and approved network paths explicitly.
Use appropriate organization and source condition keys in policies and guardrails.
Distinguish network location from identity: a private endpoint does not prove a caller is authorized.
Test expected service-to-service calls so controls do not break legitimate workloads.
takeaway: A perimeter combines several controls; no single VPC setting creates it.

title: VPC endpoint policies as a second filter
lead: An endpoint policy can limit which API calls may traverse that endpoint.
points: The endpoint policy is evaluated alongside the caller's IAM permissions and the service's resource policy when applicable.
Limit the actions, resources and principals the endpoint is intended to serve.
Private connectivity changes the path but does not grant API permission.
Check service support and the exact endpoint type when designing a perimeter.
takeaway: A restrictive endpoint policy can block traffic that an identity policy would otherwise allow.

title: IAM Access Analyzer and external sharing
lead: Analyze resource policies for access beyond the account or organization you define as trusted.
points: External access findings reveal public or cross-boundary grants on supported resources.
Unused access analysis helps identify roles or permissions to reduce.
Policy validation and custom checks can catch problems before deployment.
Review findings in context; an intended partner share still needs ownership and evidence.
takeaway: Use analysis before and after a resource-policy change, rather than relying only on manual inspection.

title: AWS Verified Access for application entry
lead: Verified Access evaluates application requests using identity and device context under configured policies.
points: Integrate an identity provider and, when appropriate, a device trust provider.
Write access policies for the private application rather than granting all users network-wide entry.
Verify application endpoint placement, DNS and traffic path separately.
Use it for application access decisions, not as a substitute for the app's own record-level authorization.
takeaway: Identity-aware access to an app and IAM permission to AWS APIs solve distinct problems.

title: Policy conditions that alter the answer
lead: The exam often turns on a condition rather than a named service.
points: aws:PrincipalOrgID can restrict a supported policy to principals in an organization.
aws:SourceVpce can bind a request to a particular VPC endpoint where supported.
aws:PrincipalTag can express verified role or session attributes.
Check whether the service inserts context keys into the request and how service calls propagate them.
takeaway: A condition key has value only when it is present and evaluated as intended for that request path.

title: Least privilege as a repeatable process
lead: Define a narrow initial role, observe actual use, and remove unnecessary permissions.
points: Separate job functions and workload identities before writing policy JSON.
Scope actions and resources using service authorization details.
Apply conditions only when their behavior has been verified.
Review Access Analyzer and activity evidence; validate changes in a safe environment.
takeaway: Least privilege requires ongoing evidence, especially when services and workload behavior change.

title: Troubleshooting AccessDenied systematically
lead: The visible error is the end of a policy evaluation path, not the diagnosis.
points: Confirm the active principal with STS identity and the exact action and resource.
Check explicit denies, then identity or resource Allows, boundaries, session policies and organization guardrails.
Check role trust separately if AssumeRole fails before the final API call.
Inspect endpoint policies, KMS key policies and condition context when the path includes them.
takeaway: Changing an IAM identity policy will not repair a missing role trust or a blocked endpoint policy.

title: Scenario: vendor access to customer data
lead: A SaaS vendor processes data for 200 customer accounts and must read a bucket in each account.
points: Create a customer-owned role with the minimum bucket permissions.
Trust the vendor's designated AWS principal and require a customer-specific external ID.
Keep the external ID associated with the correct customer account in the vendor control plane.
Audit role sessions and review the trust relationship as the integration changes.
takeaway: The external ID addresses the confused-deputy risk in a shared third-party service.

title: Scenario: workforce access to 80 accounts
lead: An enterprise IdP owns employee identity; teams need different access in development and production.
points: Integrate the external IdP with IAM Identity Center for workforce sign-in.
Provision users and groups with SCIM where supported.
Create distinct permission sets for developer and production duties.
Assign groups to account and permission-set combinations; review access when group membership changes.
takeaway: A single login experience does not imply identical privileges across accounts.

title: Scenario: consumer app with direct S3 uploads
lead: Mobile users must upload their own objects without exposing a server-side AWS access key.
points: Authenticate users with a user pool or another trusted application IdP.
Use an identity pool for limited temporary AWS credentials if direct AWS API access is required.
Constrain uploads to the caller's permitted object prefix and validate the mapping.
Consider pre-signed URLs when the backend should mediate each upload instead.
takeaway: Pick the access path based on whether the client truly needs AWS credentials.

title: Scenario: external batch servers
lead: On-premises batch workers need to write to S3 while long-term access keys are prohibited.
points: Use IAM Roles Anywhere when workers have managed X.509 identities and can operate the required PKI.
Create a trust anchor and role profile that limits which role each workload can obtain.
Grant the role only the relevant S3 write actions and prefixes.
Design certificate rotation, revocation and logging before rollout.
takeaway: Temporary credentials solve the AWS key problem; certificate governance remains an operational responsibility.

title: Scenario: a pod reads a single secret
lead: One EKS workload needs Secrets Manager access; neighboring pods must not inherit it.
points: Bind the workload's Kubernetes service account to a dedicated Pod Identity association.
Grant its IAM role read access to the one secret and required KMS decrypt permission if applicable.
Keep other service accounts separate and restrict node credential exposure.
Test the pod's actual credentials and a neighboring pod's denied request.
takeaway: The pod, rather than the node or cluster, should be the access boundary.

title: Scenario: stop unintended external access
lead: A storage policy change could expose a regulated dataset outside the organization.
points: Use an external access analyzer to detect policy grants beyond the chosen zone of trust.
Add tested organization or principal restrictions to the resource policy as appropriate.
Use VPC endpoint policy and approved path conditions for requests expected from private workloads.
Validate legitimate service principals and partner exceptions before enforcing a broad deny.
takeaway: Combine finding review with tested guardrails; an analyzer finding alone does not block a request.

title: Decision drill: which identity service?
lead: Match the caller to the credential path before looking at the application architecture.
points: Employees using many AWS accounts: IAM Identity Center with assignments.
Customer signs in to a web application: Cognito user pool or an application IdP.
Authenticated mobile user needs constrained direct AWS API calls: identity pool.
External server with a managed certificate: IAM Roles Anywhere.
takeaway: The distinction among user authentication, application authorization and AWS credentials is exam critical.

title: Decision drill: where did the Allow fail?
lead: A role has an S3 Allow, yet PutObject fails. Investigate the complete request path.
points: Is the final caller actually that role session?
Does the policy match the precise object ARN and action?
Does an SCP, boundary, session policy, endpoint policy or bucket policy block the call?
Does encryption invoke a separate KMS permission check?
takeaway: The nearest policy document is not necessarily the policy that decided the request.

title: Resource policy principal precision
lead: A grant to a role ARN and a grant directly to a role session ARN can behave differently with implicit denies.
points: Inspect the Principal value in the resource policy before applying a simplified policy-intersection rule.
A direct grant to a role session principal can bypass an implicit deny in its identity policy or session policy within the same account.
An applicable explicit Deny still overrides the grant.
Prefer the intended role and resource boundary; test policy behavior when a design depends on this exception.
takeaway: Policy evaluation has principal-specific exceptions. Never infer a final decision from one policy in isolation.

title: Identity architecture: final synthesis
lead: Identity design is a chain of authentication, temporary credentials, authorization and evidence.
points: Workforce: IdP, provisioning, Identity Center, permission set and account assignment.
Application: user token, API authorization and optional scoped AWS credentials.
Workload: platform role, OIDC or X.509 federation with short-lived sessions.
Governance: policy ceilings, data perimeter and Access Analyzer review.
takeaway: For any exam scenario, draw the caller and every trust boundary before choosing a service.
